summary: Updates RFC 3279 to specify algorithm identifiers and ASN.1 encoding for DSA and ECDSA signatures that use SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, or SHA-512. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Certificates need to name the signing method they use. This document adds names for signing methods that use stronger fingerprint math.

subtitle: Names for signing certificates with DSA or ECDSA plus the SHA-2 family of hash functions.

tldr.problem: Internet X.509 certificates and CRLs need a standard way to say which signature algorithm and hash function were used, and RFC 3279 did not cover SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512 with DSA and ECDSA.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC assigns object identifiers (OIDs) for the SHA-2 hash functions, for DSA with SHA-224 and SHA-256, and for ECDSA with all four hashes, and says how to encode them.
tldr.outcome: Certification authorities SHOULD use a SHA-2 hash, and may use SHA-1 only under a stated policy that requires it. The RFC updates RFC 3279.

today: RFC 5758 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3279. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This specification defines what goes into the signatureAlgorithm, signatureValue and signature fields of Internet X.509 certificates and certificate revocation lists (CRLs) when they are signed with DSA or ECDSA using a SHA-2 hash. Those fields are described in RFC 5280.

The document profiles three outside standards: the Secure Hash Standard (FIPS 180-3), the ECDSA standard X9.62, and the Digital Signature Standard (FIPS 186-3). It updates sections 2.1, 2.2.2 and 2.2.3 of RFC 3279. Separately, RFC 5480 updates other parts of RFC 3279.
sections.plainLanguage: A certificate carries a signature and a label saying how it was signed. This document writes down the labels for some newer signing methods.

sections.title: Hash Functions
sections.content:
Four hash functions are identified for use with DSA and ECDSA in the X.509 profile: SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512. They produce a 224-bit, 256-bit, 384-bit and 512-bit hash of the input, and are fully described in FIPS 180-3. Each gets an object identifier: id-sha224, id-sha256, id-sha384 and id-sha512.

When one of these OIDs appears in an AlgorithmIdentifier, implementations MUST accept both NULL and absent parameters as legal and equivalent encodings.

Conforming certification authority (CA) implementations SHOULD use one of the four SHA-2 hashes when generating certificates or CRLs. They MAY use SHA-1 only if they have a stated policy that requires the use of this weaker algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: A hash is a short fingerprint of a long message. Four fingerprint sizes are named here, and certificate makers are told to prefer them over the older, weaker one.

sections.title: DSA Signatures
sections.content:
The Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA) is defined in the Digital Signature Standard, FIPS 186-3. This RFC defines id-dsa-with-sha224 and id-dsa-with-sha256, which say that DSA was used with SHA-224 or SHA-256.

When either identifier appears as an AlgorithmIdentifier, the encoding SHALL omit the parameters field, so the identifier is a SEQUENCE of one component, the OID. DSA signature values are encoded as specified in RFC 3279.

A conforming CA that generates DSA signatures for certificates or CRLs MUST follow sections 4.1, 4.5 and 4.6 of FIPS 186-3. It MAY follow all requirements and recommendations of FIPS 186-3 if it has a stated policy that requires that.
sections.plainLanguage: DSA is one way to sign. The label for it carries no extra settings, only the name of the method and the fingerprint type.

sections.title: ECDSA Signatures
sections.content:
The Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) is defined in X9.62. The RFC defines ecdsa-with-SHA224, ecdsa-with-SHA256, ecdsa-with-SHA384 and ecdsa-with-SHA512.

As with DSA, the encoding MUST omit the parameters field. A conforming CA MUST name the hash algorithm explicitly with these OIDs when encoding ECDSA/SHA2 signatures in certificates and CRLs. Conforming clients that process ECDSA signatures with any SHA-2 hash MUST recognize the corresponding OIDs.

Signature value encoding is given in section 2.2.3 of RFC 3279 and in RFC 5480. A CA MUST generate ECDSA signatures following sections 7.2 and 7.3 of X9.62 or section 4.1.3 of SEC1.
sections.plainLanguage: ECDSA is another way to sign, using a different kind of math. Its labels name the fingerprint type directly, and software must understand all of them.

sections.title: The ASN.1 Module
sections.content: This RFC does not carry its own ASN.1 module. The OIDs of the SHA-2 hash algorithms are in the ASN.1 module of RFC 4055. The OIDs for DSA with SHA-224 and SHA-256 and for ECDSA with SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 are defined in the ASN.1 module of RFC 5480.
sections.plainLanguage: The formal list of names lives in two other documents, and this one just points to them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The section is short. NIST has defined appropriate use of the hash functions, in terms of algorithm strengths and expected time frames for secure use, in Special Publications 800-78-1, 800-57 and 800-107. These can guide the choice of key sizes for different security scenarios.

ANSI also provides security considerations for ECDSA in X9.62, and these may be used as a guide.
sections.plainLanguage: How strong is strong enough? The document sends readers to government guides that explain which sizes are safe for how long.
